children.name: My curiosity has always taken me toward things that cannot be explained by a single, familiar way of thinking. Since I was young, I have been fascinated by astrology, birth charts, the Five Elements, and other forms of spirituality. I found it intriguing that people could look at the same sky, the same natural world, or the same human life and create entirely different systems to understand them. As I grew older, that curiosity expanded beyond simply reading about them. I began exploring these systems for myself, tracing the meanings behind symbols, comparing different interpretations, and wondering why they have continued to shape the way people understand themselves and the world around them. That curiosity eventually led me into many other forms of exploration. These explorations may seem unrelated on the surface, but I was drawn to the same question underneath them: what can I see when I step into a different way of understanding? Like Uranus, whose extreme tilt creates seasons unlike those on any other planet in our solar system, I am drawn to experiences that shift the conditions through which I see the world. I do not explore these ideas to find one absolute answer, I explore them for what they reveal: new connections between nature and culture, different ways of understanding human experience, or simply questions I had never thought to ask. Sometimes, entering a different world of thought is enough to make a familiar world feel new.

children.name: The philosophy of the Wu Xing has long served as a cornerstone of Eastern thought. Rather than a static classification of matter, it represents a dynamic system that describes the stages of energy transformation through mutual generation and restriction. These five forces govern all phenomena in the universe, from the movement of constellations to the structural integrity of architectural works. My interest in this philosophy stems from a desire to find stability and balance. I am drawn to how it provides a predictive, grounded framework for thinking, showing that even chaotic emotions or high-stress situations are simply expressions of energy imbalance, something we have the power to adjust. This offers a solid footing, helping me view challenges as transitions between elements to proactively guide myself. A clear example of this is Tran Quoc Pagoda. More than just a historical monument, the pagoda serves as a perfect architectural embodiment of the Five Elements in motion.

children.name: Enclosing the brick and stone structures is a lush canopy of ancient trees, anchored by a massive Bodhi tree that offers sweeping shade. In the Five Elements, green represents Wood, a symbol of growth and expansion. Around the pagoda, the green canopy spreads horizontally, contrasting with the vertical rise of the tower. These two perpendicular directions create a well-balanced architectural proportion between height and width. Ancient belief held that earth energy does not travel in straight, rigid lines like stone or metal; it flows fluidly, much like a root system beneath the soil. The ancient trees here serve to retain and naturally disperse this energy. From above, the canopy forms a soft green ring enclosing the grounds. It softens and disperses the intense Yang energy radiating from the red tower, rendering the spiritual space harmonious, cool, and full of vitality.

children.name: While the red tower draws the eye upward, the golden accents throughout the pagoda ground the mind in the stillness of Earth. In classical philosophy, Earth is not simply soil; it is the center of the entire Five Elements system, maintaining equilibrium among the remaining four. Golden horizontal lacquered boards and vertical couplets are placed at the center of the worship area, where light naturally gathers. Under candlelight or sunlight, the gilded surfaces reflect brilliantly, turning the main hall into a radiant focal point that draws all attention inward. This reflects an ancient cosmological view: no matter how the four cardinal directions shift, they must revolve around a stable center. The gold at the center of Tran Quoc Pagoda serves as a reminder that regardless of how things shift, everything ultimately returns to the center to find peace.

children.name: The presence of stone balustrades and light-colored stone Buddha statues scattered across the grounds represents Metal. Here, Metal is more than just material; it represents form, structure, and crystallization, the phase where energy condenses to give clear, stable definition to matter. These white stone elements are positioned along paths, at steps, or where different spaces meet, acting as markers that define the layout. Instead of building solid perimeter walls that might feel oppressive, low stone balustrades create a soft boundary, defining the space while keeping the landscape open and airy. White stone reflects sunlight exceptionally well. Set against the deep greens of the trees and the dark hues of the water, these white stone accents act as bright points along the paths, keeping the overall composition from fading into the background.

children.name: The final element, enveloping the other four, is the expanse of West Lake, representing Water. Water here is not just a physical body of liquid, but a vast field of energy that facilitates flow. The calm lake acts as a mirror, reflecting the sky, clouds, and the pagoda's silhouette. This reflection doubles the spiritual space, creating a sense that heaven and earth are merging on the water's surface. In feng shui, a strip of land cradled by water is known as a "water-embracing" formation. This topography acts like a basin, gathering and preserving energy from dispersing. From afar, Tran Quoc Pagoda resembles a quiet, sacred island of energy standing out amidst the waters of West Lake.

children.name: Seen from above, the layout of Tran Quoc Pagoda resembles a lotus blooming in the middle of the lake. The causeway leading into the pagoda acts as the stem, while the tower cluster and main halls form the heart of the flower. This design creates a deep connection to Vietnam’s national symbol. The lotus represents the spirit of the Vietnamese people: a flower rising from mud and water while retaining its purity. By shaping the pagoda in this image, the builders subtly linked the Five Elements with a cultural ideal. Ultimately, the Five Elements serve as a bridge between the environment and human experience. This philosophy teaches that every individual exists within a larger flow of elements. Just as Tran Quoc Pagoda uses Metal to set boundaries and Water to create reflection, I draw on these principles to find balance in my own life. The philosophy demonstrates that stability does not come from total stillness, but from the harmonious interaction of all elements, much like a resilient lotus standing firm amid the moving currents of a lake.

children.name: Since childhood, the planets in my mind were always distant, cold, quiet spheres, entirely detached from the world down here. But in the eyes of the ancients, celestial bodies were never mere inanimate rock. To them, each carried a breath representing a different shade of human existence, from the softness of darkness, to the fiery heat of harvest, or the slow passage of time. Passing through changing seasons, I realized the sky continuously shifts to the rhythm of time. Whenever the air, light, and humidity alter, a certain planet imperceptibly surfaces in our thoughts. Rather than analyzing the entire solar system from a scientific standpoint, I have chosen four celestial bodies that held a powerful sway over the ancient imagination: Venus, Mars, Saturn, and the Moon. I chose them not for their size or distance, but because each seems to align naturally with a particular season of the year. As light and atmosphere shift, the sky changes its character, making us feel as though we are living under the influence of entirely different worlds.

children.name: Venus, spring and the softening of the world
children.characters: Venus, spring and the softening of the world

children.name: To open this cycle, we meet Venus, the planet of openness and solace. In astronomy, Venus is enveloped in an intensely dense atmosphere of sulfuric acid clouds that reflect light more powerfully than anything else in the solar system. This thick layer completely conceals the rugged surface beneath, presenting the planet as a luminous yet misty sphere. Much like spring in Northern Vietnam after the biting cold of winter, a thin haze and moisture weave an ethereal veil over the air, softening every street corner and every branch. The high reflectivity of Venus's atmosphere mirrors how the earth in spring diffuses a gentle light, blurring the sharp, harsh lines of colder days. Just as the sky needs the veiled clouds of Venus to welcome spring, people too need moments to shed their cold sharpness, learning to be more forgiving and gentle with themselves.

children.name: Mars, summer and the heat of space
children.characters: Mars, summer and the heat of space

children.name: Yet the universe cannot rest forever in gentleness; it demands energy to break through, and that is when the world transitions into summer through the intense language of Mars. The planet wears a distinct reddish orange hue due to a surface rich in iron oxide. It is also a world frequently swept by global dust storms that rage for months, churning and scorching the atmosphere. The rusty red of Mars mirrors the color of late summer afternoons in Vietnam, when the horizon burns a deep red, setting the day's final clouds ablaze. Its extreme dust storms reflect the sweltering heat that makes space itself seem to shimmer and distort. This explosion is an inevitable part of nature, as summer serves as a reminder that within every person lies an elemental, fierce, and raw energy. There will be seasons in life that force us to erupt, to face internal storms in order to release our inner strength rather than suppress it.

children.name: Saturn, autumn and the slowing of time
children.characters: Saturn, autumn and the slowing of time

children.name: As autumn arrives, the world dons the mantle of another planet. This is when light begins to wane, afternoons close in hurriedly, and leaves turn color. All of creation learns to slow down after the brilliant days of summer. In the ancient world, Saturn was the manifestation of time, old age, and silence. As the slowest moving planet visible to the naked eye, Saturn has always borne a distant, immensely serene presence. Amid Hanoi’s autumn, that same sense of remoteness subtly permeates the air. It lingers in the pale sunlight, the first brisk nip of cold, and the leaf strewn streets. Saturn is no longer a distant pinpoint of light, it becomes the very moment we realize time has paused, inviting us to look within.

children.name: The Moon, winter and the deeper sky
children.characters: The Moon, winter and the deeper sky

children.name: When winter settles, nightfall arrives more swiftly, and the bitter cold turns the light crisp and sharp. It is a time when people withdraw, turning their eyes upward toward the infinite void rather than down at the cluttered ground. In the ancient consciousness, the Moon was never merely the ruler of the night. People found within it the stillness of hidden things. The Moon is truly beautiful only when the world is quiet enough. Seen through the lens of winter, the sky feels a layer deeper. Winter pulls back the curtain, allowing the vast darkness to serve as a backdrop for the moonlight to shine through. Journeying through the four seasons under the guidance of these ancient celestial bodies, we come to realize at the end of the path that even in the coldest winter night, the Moon remains, like the final spark of the soul holding onto light for the vault of the sky.
